title: Introduction to type conversion and static_cast
recap: A type conversion creates a value of another type without changing the source object. Implicit conversions happen automatically, while explicit conversions state the programmer's intent.

static_cast<target_type>(expression) performs an explicit conversion. Casting a floating-point value to int discards its fractional part, while casting an integer operand to double before division preserves a fractional quotient.
objectives: Use static_cast<int> for an intentional truncating conversion.
Place static_cast<double> before division to avoid integer division.
Recognize that converting after integer division cannot restore a lost fraction.
Format the floating result with stable fixed precision.
warnings: Converting a double to int discards the fractional component rather than rounding.
Integer division loses the remainder before a later conversion can occur.
Do not use C-style casts or turn the expected results into constants.
challenge: Keep the intentional conversion of 7.75 crates to 7 whole crates. Repair averagePerTeam() so seven items divided among two teams produces 3.5 by explicitly converting an operand to double before division. Retain both static_cast forms, fixed one-decimal formatting for the average, and the deterministic no-input report.
hints: static_cast<int>(7.75) intentionally removes .75 and already gives the required whole-crate count.
Both operands are currently int when division occurs, so their remainder is discarded.
Convert items to double inside the division expression, before the / operator is evaluated.
